pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Fast & Slow Earth Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** No direct KS1 science statement; the 'slow change' strand (rock worn away by wind/water) is developed in KS2 science (Y3 Rocks; erosion) and KS2 Geography, and 'fast change' (volcanoes/earthquakes) sits in KS2 Geography. At 5–7 teach via KS1 'Working scientifically' (comparing, using information sources) as enrichment.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** Direct anchor — **2-ESS1-1**: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1].' Clarification: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1].' Assessment boundary: does NOT include quantitative measurements of timescales. CCC [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1, 2-ESS2-1].' SEP: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1].

- **Operational details:** The big idea is that Earth's surface is always changing — but at very different speeds. Some changes are sudden (a volcanic eruption or earthquake reshapes land in moments); others are so slow (wind and water wearing rock into sand over very long times) you can't watch them happen. Teach by CONTRASTING paired examples from photos/footage and sorting events into 'fast' and 'slow', then confronting the hardest part for young children: slow changes are REAL changes even though we can't see them happening — use before/after pairs (a smooth pebble was once a rough rock; a cliff that has retreated). Honour the assessment boundary: compare fast vs slow qualitatively, never quantify years. This topic ties the batch together (volcano/earthquake = fast; erosion = slow).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can give an example of a fast change and a slow change and say which is which; they are NOT expected to quantify timescales. Confront two misconceptions: 'the Earth never changes / has always looked the same', and 'only dramatic fast events count as change' (slow wearing-away is change too).
bestPractices: Teach through paired contrasts (a fast example beside a slow one) so the RATE difference is the focus, not the events in isolation
Make time the variable children control, so 'you can't watch slow change happen' is experienced, not just stated
Use before/after pairs (rough rock → smooth pebble; cliff retreated) to prove slow changes are real changes
Provide a simple fast/slow sorting task to meet the 'compare and classify' evidence directly
Honour the assessment boundary — keep it qualitative (fast vs slow), never quantify years
Draw the fast examples from this batch (eruption, earthquake) and the slow from erosion, tying the topics together
keyRepresentations: Two scenes under one shared time slider (fast scene vs slow scene)
Fast/slow sorting bins with event cards (eruption, earthquake, erosion, pebble-smoothing)
Before/after image pairs showing slow change has really happened
A simple 'rock → sand' sequence for wearing-away over long time
commonMisconceptions: 'The Earth never changes / has always looked exactly the same' — the surface is always changing, just often too slowly to see
'Only big dramatic events (eruptions/quakes) are changes' — slow wearing-away by wind and water is change too
'If you can't see it happen, it isn't really happening' — slow changes are real; before/after evidence shows it
'Slow changes are small changes' — given long enough, slow processes carve valleys and wear mountains down
'Fast changes build the land and slow changes only destroy it' — both build and wear down (keep simple: both reshape the land)

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach that Earth's surface is always changing but at very different speeds: some changes are quick (earthquakes can reshape land in moments, and volcanic eruptions can change it within hours or days) and some are so slow (wind and water wearing rock into sand) that you cannot watch them happen. The core work is contrasting a fast example beside a slow one so the difference in RATE is the focus, sorting events into 'fast' and 'slow', and using before/after evidence to prove slow changes are real changes. Keep everything qualitative — compare fast vs slow, never quantify years (per the NGSS assessment boundary).

activities.title: Same nudge, different world: a shared time control over two scenes
feedback: When the tiny nudge erupts the left scene but barely touches the right, prompt: 'Same nudge — why did one change so much and the other hardly at all?'
If the child stops dragging too soon on the slow scene, encourage: 'Keep going — slow changes need a LOT of time. Watch what happens to the rock if you keep cranking time forward.'
Once the pebble has rounded, affirm: 'The rock really did change — it just took a long, long time. That is a slow change, and it is still a real change.'
activities.rationale: A shared time control lets learners compare how much two modelled scenes change during the same elapsed time. The linked scenes and optional slider provide one proposed way to explore the crosscutting idea that things may change slowly or rapidly; their effectiveness has not been independently evaluated.
sourceClaims: CCC Stability and Change for this PE: 'Things may change slowly or rapidly'; DCI ESS1.C: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1]'
learnerActions: Look at two scenes placed side by side that share ONE time control (for example a slider or scrubber the child drags).
Give the time control the tiniest nudge and watch the left scene: a volcano erupts or an earthquake strikes, reshaping the land very quickly.
Now expect the right scene to change the same way — but notice the cliff barely moves with that same small nudge.
Keep dragging time on and on for the right scene until the cliff slowly wears back and a rough rock gradually rounds into a smooth pebble.
Say out loud which change was fast and which was slow, and agree that BOTH really changed the land.
activities.intendedInsight: Some Earth changes are sudden and some are so slow you cannot watch them happen, yet both are real changes to the land. The felt asymmetry — the same action causing wildly different amounts of change — makes the difference in rate experiential rather than just stated.

activities.title: Sort the changes: fast bin or slow bin
feedback: For these represented examples, the eruption and earthquake change the land rapidly; the cliff wearing-away, pebble smoothing and gradual dune buildup occur over a much longer time. Other instances can differ: use the conditions and time context shown.
If a slow card is called 'not a real change': 'It changes slowly, but it still changes — a rough rock really did become a smooth pebble.'
If a card is misplaced, ask: 'Would that happen in a day, or over many, many years?'
activities.rationale: Sorting can teach and check classification. Ask learners to justify a card using its described change and elapsed-time context; optionally pair the sort with the shared-time model to compare amounts of change over the same interval.
sourceClaims: 2-ESS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1]'; clarification names volcanic explosions and earthquakes (quick) and erosion of rocks (slow); assessment excludes quantitative timescales
learnerActions: Take event cards showing a sudden eruption, a sudden earthquake, gradual cliff wearing-away, gradual pebble smoothing and gradual sand-dune buildup. Use each card’s described conditions and time context, rather than assuming every instance of a process has the same speed.
Place each card into a 'fast' bin or a 'slow' bin.
For at least one card, say why it goes where it goes ('the eruption changed the land quickly, so it's fast').
Answer a 'Which change is slow?' question and a reinforcement question: 'Are the slow changes still real changes to the land?'
activities.intendedInsight: In these card examples, the eruption and earthquake are fast changes, and the wearing-away and dune buildup are slow changes. Both kinds genuinely reshape the land. Classifying events can check whether a child compares quick and slow changes.

activities.title: Before and after: proving slow change is real
feedback: When a difference is found: 'Good spotting — that part of the cliff is gone now. Something like waves, water or wind slowly wore it away.'
If the child says the slow pair looks 'the same', point to a specific difference: 'Look here — is this edge in the same place in both pictures?'
Reinforce: 'We didn't see it move, but the two pictures are different — so it really did change.'
activities.rationale: Before/after pairs address the misconception that 'if you can't see it happen, it isn't really happening' by supplying observable evidence of slow change. A still pair cannot by itself convey how fast or slow the change was, which is why pairs are tagged fast/slow and paired with the time-control activity; this is a scaffold for the 'real change' idea, not a substitute for experiencing rate.
sourceClaims: 2-ESS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1]'; clarification names volcanic explosions and earthquakes (quick) and erosion of rocks (slow); assessment excludes quantitative timescales
learnerActions: Look at paired before/after images — for example a cliff that has retreated, or a rough rock that has become a smooth round pebble; alongside a fast pair such as land before and after an eruption.
Tap or point to each spot that is different and name what changed.

Use the source’s time context, such as moments later or a long time later, to tag each pair as fast or slow. If no elapsed-time context is available, state that the images show a change but do not establish its speed.
For the slow pair, answer: 'How do we know this really changed if we never watched it happen?'
activities.intendedInsight: Even when we cannot watch a change happen moment to moment, comparing a 'before' and an 'after' is evidence that the change is real. Slow changes leave proof behind.

activities.title: Talk it through: is a wearing-away cliff still changing?
feedback: If the child says water is too soft to change rock: 'Think of a smooth round pebble — it started rough. What made it smooth? Moving water tumbled it against sand and other stones again and again, over a very long time.'
If the child still doubts that gentle forces matter, point to everyday proof: 'Look at worn-down stone steps — many feet treading over many years wore the hard stone away. Slow, but real.'
If they deny the cliff is changing: 'It changes too slowly to watch, but photos taken a long time apart would look different — so it really is changing.'
Affirm fresh correct examples: 'Yes, that's another slow change — nicely spotted.'
activities.rationale: Asking the child to generate and justify their own examples moves beyond recognition into independent explanation, targeting the crux misconception that only dramatic events count as change. Spoken dialogue can support this reasoning; for this age the hands-on sort-and-time activities may deliver the rate contrast more concretely, so talk is best used to probe and extend understanding. This is a proposed use, not an efficacy-tested one.
learnerActions: Respond to prompts such as 'Can you think of a fast change to the land? A slow one?'
Explain whether a cliff that is slowly wearing away is still changing, and why.
Give a fresh example of each kind of change in your own words.
Answer the probe: 'If you photographed a cliff today and again a long time from now, would they look the same?'
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the idea into your own words — naming examples and defending that a slow, gentle process genuinely changes the land — consolidates and reveals understanding. Recognition in a sort does not by itself show a child can produce and explain examples; this activity targets that production.

constraints: Keep all comparisons qualitative: compare fast vs slow and 'a long time' vs 'a moment', but never ask children to quantify timescales in years — the NGSS 2-ESS1-1 assessment boundary excludes quantitative measurement of timescales.
Draw fast examples from eruptions and earthquakes and slow examples from erosion/wearing-away, so the topic ties to the wider volcanoes & earthquakes material.

A sorting/classification task can check whether a child compares quick and slow changes, but does not by itself elicit the felt sense of how different the rates are; use it alongside, not instead of, an activity where the child controls time.

Before/after pairs show that change occurred. Include qualitative elapsed-time context to compare rates; an undated pair alone does not establish speed. A shared time-control model is an optional additional representation.
Keep 'both build and wear down' simple: say both kinds of change reshape the land, rather than assigning 'building' only to fast events and 'destroying' only to slow ones.
Target the key misconceptions explicitly: that the Earth never changes, that only dramatic events count as change, that unseen slow change isn't real, and that slow changes are only small.
Keep the slider/panel, sort and dialogue as proposed, complementary scaffolds; do not present any one medium as the only route to understanding or as proven more effective than another.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a side-by-side time-control interactive as 'ideal' and dialogue and 3D as 'poor/possible'; those are catalog fit rankings, not evidence of comparative efficacy. The activities here are preserved as complementary proposals with their affordances and limits stated, rather than ranked.

The claim that erosion wears rock into sand, that cliffs retreat, and that pebbles and stone steps are smoothed/worn by water or use over long time is standard primary-science content consistent with the cited NGSS clarification; actual rates depend on rock type and conditions, but since the topic stays qualitative no quantitative claim is made or needed.
One source (DfE KS2 placement) is marked verified:false in the row; the UK curriculum placement note is retained only as context and not relied on for the US-anchored teaching objective.

The original assessment probe phrased the thought experiment as 'again in fifty years'; it was kept as a qualitative 'a long time from now' framing to avoid implying a timescale measurement, while still matching the original intent. Either phrasing is a hypothetical, not a quantification the child must produce.

The 2-ESS1-1 'several sources' claim was removed from activity 1 because its core assertion supports the evidence/classify tasks (activities 2–3) rather than activity 1's experiential-rate principle, which the CCC claim directly supports.

probeDeeper: Which took longer to happen — the volcano changing the land, or the cliff wearing away?
If you photographed the cliff today and again in fifty years, would they look the same?
Can you think of another fast change and another slow change to the land?
A pebble on the beach is smooth and round. What made it that shape — something fast or something slow?
assess.correctAnswer: The volcano is a fast change (it can reshape the land in a day); the cliff wearing away is a slow change (it takes many years). And yes — even gentle water and wind really do wear away solid rock, but so slowly that we can't watch it happen.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only big dramatic events change the land; gentle water or wind can't change solid rock
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show worn stone steps or a smooth round pebble — slow change adds up over very many years.
errorPatterns.distractor: The waves can't really change solid rock — only the volcano changes the land.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the cliff isn't really changing, or that water is too soft to wear rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: If you can't see it moving, nothing is happening ('the cliff looks the same, so it's not changing')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a photo now with one from long ago; the change is real but too slow to see moment to moment.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing is happening to the cliff — it looks the same.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates 'can't watch it change' with 'not changing at all'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Landforms like mountains and cliffs were always exactly as they are now
errorPatterns.nextMove: The land has a history and keeps changing — sometimes fast, sometimes slow.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the land was ever different in the past.

responseLevels.gap: Can't sort fast vs slow, or denies that gentle/slow processes change the land at all.
responseLevels.full: Sorts quick vs slow with examples AND explains that slow processes really do change the land over long time even though we can't watch it, giving a fresh example of each.
responseLevels.partial: Labels the volcano fast and the cliff slow but treats the slow change as 'not really happening', or can't explain the difference.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A cliff by the sea slowly wears away as waves hit it, year after year. A volcano can change the land in a single day. Which change is fast and which is slow — and can something as gentle as water really change solid rock?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The crux is whether the child accepts that a slow, gentle process genuinely changes rock over long time. Sorting fast vs slow is easy; a child who thinks only dramatic events change the land will deny the slow one counts — so affirming the gentle change is real is what separates them.
